1.explanation: Both the SpriteInfo class and the DirectionPicker component render the grouped icon‐button toggles for ‘show/hide’ and the rotation styles, respectively. In SpriteInfo.render, the two <div> elements with classNames(styles.radio…) wrap the show/hide icons and apply styles.isActive when selected — this is where the background styling must change. In the DirectionPicker function, each <button> uses classNames(styles.iconButton, {[styles.active]: …}) to mark the selected rotation style. These are the exact locations where the UI applies active/inactive styles based on color alone; updating these class rules (or adding new background classes) will implement the background‐color change needed for colorblind accessibility.
1.bug_scenario: The show/hide toggle and rotation‐style buttons currently rely on icon color fill (blue vs. gray) to indicate which option is active. In grayscale (or for colorblind users) both filled and unfilled icons appear similar and it’s impossible to tell which option is selected (as shown in the first set of images). The desired behavior is to use a distinct background color (blue for active, white for inactive) behind the button’s icon so that selection is clear regardless of color vision (as shown in the proposed design in the second image).

2.explanation: Both the show/hide switch and the rotation‐style buttons rely on toggling an “active” CSS class on the icon element itself, changing only the icon’s fill color. To implement the colorblind‐friendly design, we need to modify where and how the active state CSS class is applied—specifically in SpriteInfo.render for the show/hide icons and in the DirectionPicker component’s buttonRow for rotation styles—so that the background of the selected button changes color instead of (or in addition to) tinting the icon.
2.bug_scenario: In the current settings UI, state is indicated solely by coloring the show/hide and rotation‐style icons filled versus grayed out. In color this works, but in grayscale (or for colorblind users) the two icons look identical, so you can’t tell which option is active. The proposed design instead highlights the selected button with a colored background and leaves the unselected button with a white background, making the active state clear even without color.
